A wetland is a type of land that is soaked in water — either all the time or for a significant part of the year — and because of that water, it supports a very specific kind of soil, plants, and wildlife. Think of it as the in-between world: not quite dry land, not quite a lake or a river, but something in the middle.

The word is exactly what it sounds like: land that is wet.
What Officially Makes a Place a Wetland?

Not every muddy patch of ground is a wetland. Scientists use three specific criteria together to define one:

  1. Water (Hydrology): The land must be flooded or thoroughly soaked with water for at least part of the year — sometimes permanently, sometimes seasonally (say, during the monsoon months).
  2. Waterlogged Soil (Hydric Soil): When soil sits underwater for a long time, it changes. Oxygen gets pushed out, and the soil turns dark, soft, and sometimes smells like rotten eggs. This kind of soil is called hydric soil, and it's a signature marker of a wetland.
  3. Water-Tolerant Plants (Hydrophytes): Most land plants die if their roots stay submerged for too long. Wetlands, however, are home to plants specially built to survive — and even thrive — with their roots in waterlogged ground. Reeds, cattails, water lilies, and mangrove trees are classic examples.

All three features must be present (at least at some point during the year) for a piece of land to be called a wetland. Remove the water permanently, and over time the soil and plants change too — and it stops being a wetland.
The Water in a Wetland

The water in a wetland can be:

  • Fresh (like in inland marshes and bogs)
  • Salty (like in coastal mangrove swamps)
  • Brackish — a mix of fresh and salty (like in estuaries, where rivers meet the sea)

The water itself can come from many sources: rainfall, rivers overflowing their banks, groundwater seeping up from underground, tides, or snowmelt.
Types of Wetlands

Wetlands come in several forms, each with its own character:

Marshes are probably what most people picture first. They are shallow, open wetlands dominated by soft plants like grasses, reeds, and sedges (not trees). The ground is saturated or covered by shallow water. Marshes can be freshwater (found inland near rivers and lakes) or saltwater (found along coastlines). The Florida Everglades in the United States is one of the most famous freshwater marshes in the world.

Swamps are like marshes, but dominated by trees and shrubs instead of grasses. If you imagine a moody, tree-filled area with water between the trunks, that's a swamp. The trees growing here are specially adapted to have their roots in water. Cypress swamps (freshwater) and mangrove swamps (saltwater, found in tropical coastlines) are well-known examples. The Sundarbans — straddling India and Bangladesh — is the world's largest mangrove swamp.

Bogs are very different in character. They form in cool, rainy climates and are fed almost entirely by rainwater — which means they receive very few nutrients. The ground is spongy and acidic, carpeted with a thick, moisture-holding moss called sphagnum moss. Partially decomposed plant matter builds up over centuries into a thick, dark, squishy material called peat. Bogs are home to some unusual plants, like carnivorous sundews and pitcher plants, which catch insects to compensate for the lack of nutrients in the soil. Ireland and Scotland are famous for their bogs.

Fens are closely related to bogs but are fed by groundwater flowing through the ground, which brings in more minerals and nutrients. They are less acidic than bogs. Like bogs, fens also accumulate peat. Together, bogs and fens are grouped under the term peatlands.

Floodplains are low-lying stretches of land beside rivers that get regularly flooded when the river overflows. During floods, they temporarily become wetlands. The Amazon River floodplain is one of the most extensive in the world.

Estuaries are coastal wetlands where a river meets the sea. Here, fresh river water and salty ocean water mix, creating a brackish environment that is incredibly rich in life. Estuaries serve as nurseries for many species of fish and shellfish.
Where Are Wetlands Found?

Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica. They are found:

  • Along rivers and their banks
  • Around lakes and ponds
  • Along coastlines (especially in tropical and subtropical areas)
  • In cold northern and arctic regions (where frozen ground, called permafrost, traps water at the surface)
  • Tucked inside forests

The Pantanal in South America (spanning parts of Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay) is the world's largest tropical wetland — a vast, seasonally flooded plain bigger than many countries. The Okavango Delta in Botswana is a famous inland delta that floods each year, turning a desert region into a wildlife paradise.
Life in a Wetland

Wetlands are among the most biologically rich places on Earth — often called biodiversity hotspots. They are home to a staggering variety of life:

Plants: Water lilies, lotus, cattails, bulrushes, reeds, sedges, sphagnum moss, mangroves, cypress trees, and carnivorous plants like pitcher plants and sundews.

Birds: Wetlands are especially beloved by birds. Herons, egrets, kingfishers, pelicans, flamingos, ducks, geese, cranes, storks, and spoonbills all depend heavily on wetlands for feeding and breeding. Many migratory birds use wetlands as essential rest stops during their long journeys across continents.

Fish and shellfish: A huge number of fish species — including many that humans eat commercially — breed and grow in wetlands. Shrimp, crabs, and oysters also depend on coastal wetlands like estuaries.

Amphibians: Frogs, toads, newts, and salamanders are quintessential wetland creatures. They need water to reproduce (their eggs must stay moist) and are strong indicators of a wetland's health.

Reptiles: Alligators, crocodiles, caimans, turtles, and water snakes are common in many wetlands.

Mammals: Otters, beavers, water voles, hippos, capybaras, and in some regions even tigers (the Sundarbans) make their homes in or near wetlands.

Insects: Dragonflies and damselflies are iconic wetland insects. Mosquitoes, water beetles, and countless other invertebrates also live there, forming a crucial part of the food web.
Why Wetlands Matter — Their Role in Nature and for Humans

Wetlands are sometimes poetically called the "kidneys of the landscape" because, just as kidneys filter waste from our blood, wetlands filter and purify water flowing through them. But their value goes far beyond that:

1. Water Filtration
As water flows slowly through a wetland, the plants, soil, and microorganisms absorb and break down pollutants — including excess fertilizers from farms, sediment, and even some heavy metals. By the time water exits a wetland, it is significantly cleaner. This is an enormously valuable service, essentially a free water treatment system provided by nature.

2. Flood Control
Wetlands act like giant sponges. When heavy rainfall or river flooding occurs, wetlands absorb enormous amounts of excess water and release it slowly over time. This dramatically reduces the peak of floods downstream, protecting towns and farmland. Destroying wetlands — as has happened widely — directly worsens the severity of floods.

3. Carbon Storage
Peatlands (bogs and fens) are among the most important carbon stores on Earth. When plant matter partially decomposes and builds up as peat over thousands of years, the carbon that was in those plants gets locked away underground instead of being released into the atmosphere. Peatlands cover only about 3% of the Earth's land surface, yet they store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. When peatlands are drained or burned, that stored carbon is released as CO₂, contributing significantly to climate change.

4. Shoreline and Storm Protection
Coastal wetlands — especially mangrove forests and salt marshes — form a natural barrier between the sea and the land. They absorb wave energy during storms and reduce coastal erosion. Regions with healthy mangroves fare significantly better during tsunamis and hurricanes than those where mangroves have been cleared.

5. Groundwater Replenishment
Wetlands help refill underground water reserves (aquifers) by allowing water to seep slowly into the ground. These aquifers are vital sources of drinking water for millions of people.

6. Supporting Food and Livelihoods
Billions of people around the world rely on wetlands for food (fish, shellfish, rice grown in flooded paddies), water, materials like reeds for construction and weaving, and livelihoods related to fishing and tourism.

7. Biodiversity Support
Though wetlands cover only about 6% of Earth's land surface, they support roughly 40% of the world's species — an extraordinary concentration of life.
Wetlands and Human History

Humans have lived alongside and within wetlands for thousands of years. Many ancient civilizations thrived near wetlands — using them for fishing, growing crops in flooded fields, harvesting reeds, and traveling by boat through watery landscapes.

However, throughout the 20th century (and earlier), vast areas of wetlands were deliberately drained to create farmland, build cities, and extract peat for fuel. It is estimated that more than half of the world's wetlands have been lost since 1900 — an enormous and largely irreversible loss.

Today, the world has woken up to how critical wetlands are. The Ramsar Convention, an international treaty signed in 1971 (named after the city of Ramsar in Iran where it was agreed upon), created a global framework for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Countries that sign it commit to protecting designated wetlands of international importance, known as "Ramsar Sites." There are now thousands of such protected sites around the world.
Threats to Wetlands Today

Despite growing awareness, wetlands continue to face serious threats:

  • Drainage for agriculture and urban development — still the biggest threat globally
  • Pollution — runoff from farms (fertilizers and pesticides) and industrial discharge damage wetland ecosystems
  • Invasive species — non-native plants and animals introduced into wetlands can outcompete native species and alter the ecosystem
  • Climate change — changes in rainfall patterns, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels (which can drown coastal wetlands), and thawing permafrost all threaten wetlands worldwide
  • Water diversion — dams and irrigation projects upstream can reduce or cut off the water supply that wetlands depend on
A Quick Summary

What it isLand saturated with water (permanently or seasonally)
Three defining featuresWater + hydric soil + water-tolerant plants
Main typesMarshes, swamps, bogs, fens, floodplains, estuaries
Water typeFresh, salty, or brackish
Key rolesWater filtration, flood control, carbon storage, biodiversity, shoreline protection
StatusOver 50% lost globally since 1900; now actively protected

In short: a wetland is not just soggy ground. It is one of the most productive, life-sustaining, and protective ecosystems on Earth — a place where the meeting of water and land creates conditions unlike anywhere else, supporting extraordinary biodiversity and performing vital services that benefit the entire planet, including every human being on it.
